analysis.one_liner: Requires the Interior Department to sell off certain federal lands in ten western states at fair market value.
analysis.headline: The bill to sell off identified federal lands cleared a House committee by a 23-19 vote but was never voted on by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Interior Department to sell, by competitive auction, federal lands in ten western states that were identified in 1997 as suitable for disposal. The sales would have to be at fair market value as set by an independent appraiser, and the proceeds would go straight to the Treasury to pay down the national debt. The bill cleared the House Natural Resources Committee by a narrow 23-19 vote in early 2014 but never received a vote from the full House, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of the land — ranching, development, and investment interests in ten western states — would gain the chance to acquire federal land through competitive sale. Proceeds would reduce the national debt, a diffuse public benefit, but the land itself, currently open to everyone, would become private property.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the Secretary of the Interior to offer the identified lands for competitive sale at not less than fair market value, set by an independent appraiser.
All net proceeds from the sales must be deposited directly into the Treasury for reduction of the public debt.
The bill excludes lands needed for state selection, tribal allotments, local government use, and recreation and public purpose conveyances, and respects valid existing rights.

analysis.who_pays: Americans who use public lands in those states would permanently lose access to whatever parcels are sold, and the federal treasury loses the land's ongoing value; the debt-reduction proceeds would be a one-time payment.

drawbacks.text: Once sold, the land is gone from public ownership for good — hunting, fishing, grazing, and recreation access that Americans enjoy on federal land today could be closed off by new private owners.
The bill directs the Interior Department to sell the land rather than letting land managers decide parcel by parcel whether disposal still makes sense, even though the 1997 list is many years old.

Supporters would note the proceeds go to debt reduction and the sales happen at appraised fair market value, so taxpayers are paid — but the payment is one-time, while the public loses the land indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safeguards — competitive bidding, independent appraisal, and debt reduction — make the sale honest, but the underlying trade is one-sided: land held in common for everyone gets sold to whoever can pay, and the public loses hunting, grazing, and recreation access permanently. Money from the sale is a one-time gain set against a permanent loss of public property.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Natural Resources Committee by a 23-19 vote and was placed on the House calendar, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in July 2013 with no cosponsors and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.
A subcommittee held a hearing in October 2013, and the full committee voted 23-19 on January 28, 2014 to order the bill reported.
The committee reported the bill on April 10, 2014 and it was placed on the Union Calendar, but no floor vote ever occurred before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's land stayed public: because the bill never got a floor vote, no federal land was sold. Buyers who would have gained from the mandated sales got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jason Chaffetz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House Natural Resources Committee.

for.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill after a 23-19 committee vote and placed it on the Union Calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote, the 23-19 committee vote to report the bill, showed a narrow split, with the bill's sole sponsor a Republican and no cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Land purchasers — ranchers, developers, and investors in the West
industries.note: The bill creates a stock of federal land that must be sold at appraised fair market value, giving private buyers a chance to acquire property that is currently off the market.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and hunting/fishing users of public land
industries.note: Land now open to the public could be closed off or charged for by new private owners once sold. There is no requirement that access be preserved after disposal.
